    & {{\mathtt{local}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots ~~|~~ \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{local}’}~~{{{\mathtt{valtype}}}_{{I}}^\ast}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & {(\mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{local}’}~~{{\mathtt{valtype}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’})^\ast} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Functions can be defined as imports or exports inline:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{import}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{import}’}~~{{\mathtt{name}}^{2}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’}~~{{\mathtt{typeuse}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{import}’}~~{{\mathtt{name}}^{2}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~{{\mathtt{typeuse}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \end{array}
    } \\[0.8ex]
    & {{\mathtt{export}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~{{\mathit{id}}^?}{:}{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{export}’}~~{\mathtt{name}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’}~~\dots~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}} \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~{\mathit{id}'}{:}{\mathtt{id}}~~\dots~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{export}’}~~{\mathtt{name}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~{\mathtt{id}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \end{array} & & \\
    \multicolumn{3}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    \quad \mbox{if}~ {{\mathit{id}}^?} = {\mathit{id}'} \lor {{\mathit{id}}^?} = \epsilon \land {\mathit{id}'} \notin {I}{.}\mathsf{funcs} \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

The latter abbreviation can be applied repeatedly, if “`\dots`” contains additional export clauses. Consequently, a function declaration can contain any number of exports, possibly followed by an import.

## Data Segments

Data segments allow for an optional memory index to identify the memory to initialize. The data is written as a string, which may be split up into a possibly empty sequence of individual string literals.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{data}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{data}’}~~{{\mathit{id}}^?}{:}{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~{b^\ast}{:}{\mathtt{datastring}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    (\mathsf{data}~{b^\ast}~\mathsf{passive}, \{ \mathsf{datas}~({{\mathit{id}}^?}) \}) \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{data}’}~~{{\mathit{id}}^?}{:}{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{memuse}}}_{{I}}~~e{:}{{\mathtt{offsetexpr}}}_{{I}}~~{b^\ast}{:}{\mathtt{datastring}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    (\mathsf{data}~{b^\ast}~(\mathsf{active}~x~e), \{ \mathsf{datas}~({{\mathit{id}}^?}) \}) \\
    \end{array}
    } \\[0.8ex]
    & {\mathtt{datastring}} & ::= & {{b^\ast}^\ast}{:}{{\mathtt{string}}^\ast} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & {\bigoplus}\, {{b^\ast}^\ast} \\[0.8ex]
    & {{\mathtt{memuse}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{memory}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{memidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & x \\
    & {{\mathtt{offsetexpr}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{offset}’}~~e{:}{{\mathtt{expr}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & e \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### Abbreviations

As an abbreviation, a single folded instruction may occur in place of the offset of an active segment:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{offsetexpr}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{foldedinstr}}}_{{I}} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{offset}’}~~{{\mathtt{foldedinstr}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Also, a memory use can be omitted, defaulting to `0`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{memuse}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots ~~|~~ \epsilon & \quad\equiv\quad{} & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{memory}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{0}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

As another abbreviation, data segments may also be specified inline with memory definitions; see the respective section.

## Element Segments

Element segments allow for an optional table index to identify the table to initialize.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{elem}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{elem}’}~~{{\mathit{id}}^?}{:}{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~({\mathit{rt}}, {e^\ast}){:}{{\mathtt{elemlist}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    (\mathsf{elem}~{\mathit{rt}}~{e^\ast}~\mathsf{passive}, \{ \mathsf{elems}~({{\mathit{id}}^?}) \}) \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{elem}’}~~{{\mathit{id}}^?}{:}{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{tableuse}}}_{{I}}~~{e'}{:}{{\mathtt{offsetexpr}}}_{{I}}~~({\mathit{rt}}, {e^\ast}){:}{{\mathtt{elemlist}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    (\mathsf{elem}~{\mathit{rt}}~{e^\ast}~(\mathsf{active}~x~{e'}), \{ \mathsf{elems}~({{\mathit{id}}^?}) \}) \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{elem}’}~~{{\mathit{id}}^?}{:}{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{declare}’}~~({\mathit{rt}}, {e^\ast}){:}{{\mathtt{elemlist}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    (\mathsf{elem}~{\mathit{rt}}~{e^\ast}~\mathsf{declare}, \{ \mathsf{elems}~({{\mathit{id}}^?}) \}) \\
    \end{array}
    } \\[0.8ex]
    & {{\mathtt{elemlist}}}_{{I}} & ::= & {\mathit{rt}}{:}{{\mathtt{reftype}}}_{{I}}~~{e^\ast}{:}{\mathtt{list}}({{\mathtt{elemexpr}}}_{{I}}) & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & ({\mathit{rt}}, {e^\ast}) \\
    & {{\mathtt{elemexpr}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{item}’}~~e{:}{{\mathtt{expr}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & e \\[0.8ex]
    & {{\mathtt{tableuse}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{table}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{tableidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & x \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### Abbreviations

As an abbreviation, a single folded instruction may occur in place of the offset of an active element segment or as an element expression:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{elemexpr}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{foldedinstr}}}_{{I}} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{item}’}~~{{\mathtt{foldedinstr}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Also, the element list may be written as just a sequence of function indices:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{elemlist}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots ~~|~~ \mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~{x^\ast}{:}{{{\mathtt{funcidx}}}_{{I}}^\ast} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{ref}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’}~~{(\mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{ref.func}’}~~{{\mathtt{funcidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’})^\ast} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

A table use can be omitted, defaulting to `0`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{tableuse}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots ~~|~~ \epsilon & \quad\equiv\quad{} & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{table}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{0}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Furthermore, for backwards compatibility with earlier versions of WebAssembly, if the table use is omitted, the `\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}` keyword can be omitted as well.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{elem}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \dots \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{elem}’}~~{{\mathtt{offsetexpr}}}_{{I}}~~{\mathtt{list}}({{\mathtt{funcidx}}}_{{I}})~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{elem}’}~~{{\mathtt{offsetexpr}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~{\mathtt{list}}({{\mathtt{funcidx}}}_{{I}})~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

As yet another abbreviation, element segments may also be specified inline with table definitions; see the respective section.

## Start Function

A start function is defined in terms of its index.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{start}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{start}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{funcidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & (\mathsf{start}~x, \{  \}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

At most one start function may occur in a module, which is ensured by a suitable side condition on the `{\mathtt{module}}` grammar.

## Imports

The external type in imports can bind a symbolic tag, global, memory, or function identifier.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{import}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{import}’}~~{\mathit{nm}}_1{:}{\mathtt{name}}~~{\mathit{nm}}_2{:}{\mathtt{name}}~~({\mathit{xt}}, {I'}){:}{{\mathtt{externtype}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & (\mathsf{import}~{\mathit{nm}}_1~{\mathit{nm}}_2~{\mathit{xt}}, {I'}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### Abbreviations

As an abbreviation, imports may also be specified inline with tag, global, memory, table, or function definitions; see the respective sections.

## Exports

The syntax for exports mirrors their abstract syntax directly.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{export}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{export}’}~~{\mathit{nm}}{:}{\mathtt{name}}~~{\mathit{xx}}{:}{{\mathtt{externidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & (\mathsf{export}~{\mathit{nm}}~{\mathit{xx}}, \{  \}) \\[0.8ex]
    & {{\mathtt{externidx}}}_{{I}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{tag}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{tagidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & \mathsf{tag}~x \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{global}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{globalidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & \mathsf{global}~x \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{memory}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{memidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & \mathsf{memory}~x \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{table}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{tableidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & \mathsf{table}~x \\
    & & | & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{func}’}~~x{:}{{\mathtt{funcidx}}}_{{I}}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & \mathsf{func}~x \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### Abbreviations

As an abbreviation, exports may also be specified inline with tag, global, memory, table, or function definitions; see the respective sections.

## Modules

A module consists of a sequence of *declarations* that can occur in any order.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}}
    & {\mathit{decl}} & ::= & {\mathit{type}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{import}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{tag}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{global}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{mem}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{table}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{func}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{data}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{elem}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{start}} ~~|~~ {\mathit{export}} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

All declarations and their respective bound identifiers scope over the entire module, including the text preceding them. A module itself may optionally bind an identifier that names the module. The name serves a documentary role only.

Note

Tools may include the module name in the name section of the binary format.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {{\mathtt{decl}}}_{{I}} & ::= & {{\mathtt{type}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{import}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{tag}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{global}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{mem}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{table}}}_{{I}} \\
    & & | & {{\mathtt{func}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{data}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{elem}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{start}}}_{{I}} ~~|~~ {{\mathtt{export}}}_{{I}} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {\mathtt{module}} & ::= & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{module}’}~~{{\mathtt{id}}^?}~~{({\mathit{decl}}, {I})^\ast}{:}{{{\mathtt{decl}}}_{{I'}}^\ast}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad{} & & \\
    &&& \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    \mathsf{module}~{{\mathit{type}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{import}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{tag}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{global}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{mem}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{table}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{func}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{data}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{elem}}^\ast}~{{\mathit{start}}^?}~{{\mathit{export}}^\ast} & & \\
    \multicolumn{3}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    \quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    \mbox{if}~ {I'} = {\bigoplus}\, {{I}^\ast} \\
    {\land}~ {\vdash}\, {I'} : \mathsf{ok} \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{type}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{types}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{import}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{imports}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{tag}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{tags}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{global}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{globals}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{mem}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{mems}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{table}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{tables}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{func}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{funcs}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{data}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{datas}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{elem}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{elems}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{start}}^?} = {\mathrm{starts}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {{\mathit{export}}^\ast} = {\mathrm{exports}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    {\land}~ {\mathrm{ordered}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) \\
    \end{array} \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

where `{\mathrm{types}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast})`, `{\mathrm{imports}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast})`, `{\mathrm{tags}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast})`, etc., extract the sequence of types, imports, tags, etc., contained in `{{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}`, respectively. The auxiliary predicate `{\mathrm{ordered}}` checks that no imports occur after the first definition of a tag, global, memory, table, or function in a sequence of declarations:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}lcl@{}l@{}}
    {\mathrm{ordered}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) & = & \mathsf{true} & \quad \mbox{if}~ {\mathrm{imports}}({{\mathit{decl}}^\ast}) = \epsilon \\
    {\mathrm{ordered}}({{\mathit{decl}}_1^\ast}~{\mathit{import}}~{{\mathit{decl}}_2^\ast}) & = & & \\
    \multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\quad
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    {\mathrm{imports}}({{\mathit{decl}}_1^\ast}) = \epsilon \land {\mathrm{tags}}({{\mathit{decl}}_1^\ast}) = \epsilon \land {\mathrm{globals}}({{\mathit{decl}}_1^\ast}) = \epsilon \land {\mathrm{mems}}({{\mathit{decl}}_1^\ast}) = \epsilon \land {\mathrm{tables}}({{\mathit{decl}}_1^\ast}) = \epsilon \land {\mathrm{funcs}}({{\mathit{decl}}_1^\ast}) = \epsilon \\
    \end{array}
    } \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### Abbreviations

In a source file, the toplevel `\mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{module}’}~~\dots~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’}` surrounding the module body may be omitted.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}l@{}l@{}}
    & {\mathtt{module}} & ::= & \dots ~~|~~ {{{\mathtt{decl}}}_{{I}}^\ast} & \quad\equiv\quad{} & \mbox{‘\texttt{{(}}’}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{module}’}~~{{{\mathtt{decl}}}_{{I}}^\ast}~~\mbox{‘\texttt{{)}}’} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

# Embedding

A WebAssembly implementation will typically be *embedded* into a *host* environment. An *embedder* implements the connection between such a host environment and the WebAssembly semantics as defined in the main body of this specification. An embedder is expected to interact with the semantics in well-defined ways.

This section defines a suitable interface to the WebAssembly semantics in the form of entry points through which an embedder can access it. The interface is intended to be complete, in the sense that an embedder does not need to reference other functional parts of the WebAssembly specification directly.

Note

On the other hand, an embedder does not need to provide the host environment with access to all functionality defined in this interface. For example, an implementation may not support parsing of the text format.

## Types

In the description of the embedder interface, syntactic classes from the abstract syntax and the runtime’s abstract machine are used as names for variables that range over the possible objects from that class. Hence, these syntactic classes can also be interpreted as types.

For numeric parameters, notation like `i:\mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}` is used to specify a symbolic name in addition to the respective value range.

## Booleans

Interface operation that are predicates return Boolean values:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{llll}
    \def\mathdef139#1{{}}\mathdef139{Boolean} & \mathit{bool} &::=& \mathit{false} ~|~ \mathit{true} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Exceptions and Errors

Invoking an exported function may throw or propagate exceptions, expressed by an auxiliary syntactic class:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{llll}
    \def\mathdef139#1{{}}\mathdef139{exception} & \mathit{exception} &::=& \mathsf{exception}~\mathit{exnaddr} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

The exception address `exnaddr` identifies the exception thrown.

Failure of an interface operation is also indicated by an auxiliary syntactic class:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{llll}
    \def\mathdef139#1{{}}\mathdef139{error} & \mathit{error} &::=& \mathsf{error} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

In addition to the error conditions specified explicitly in this section, such as invalid arguments or exceptions and traps resulting from execution, implementations may also return errors when specific implementation limitations are reached.

Note

Errors are abstract and unspecific with this definition. Implementations can refine it to carry suitable classifications and diagnostic messages.

## Pre- and Post-Conditions

Some operations state *pre-conditions* about their arguments or *post-conditions* about their results. It is the embedder’s responsibility to meet the pre-conditions. If it does, the post conditions are guaranteed by the semantics.

In addition to pre- and post-conditions explicitly stated with each operation, the specification adopts the following conventions for runtime objects (`\mathit{store}`, `\mathit{moduleinst}`, addresses):

- Every runtime object passed as a parameter must be valid per an implicit pre-condition.

- Every runtime object returned as a result is valid per an implicit post-condition.

Note

As long as an embedder treats runtime objects as abstract and only creates and manipulates them through the interface defined here, all implicit pre-conditions are automatically met.

## Store

### `\mathrm{store\_init}() : \mathit{store}`

1.  Return the empty store.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{store\_init}() &=& \{ \} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Modules

### `\mathrm{module\_decode}(\mathit{byte}^\ast) : \mathit{module} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  If there exists a derivation for the byte sequence `\mathit{byte}^\ast` as a `\mathtt{module}` according to the binary grammar for modules, yielding a module `m`, then return `m`.

2.  Else, return `\mathsf{error}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{module\_decode}(b^\ast) &=& m && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathtt{module} \stackrel\ast\Longrightarrow m{:}b^\ast) \\
    \mathrm{module\_decode}(b^\ast) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{module\_parse}(\mathit{char}^\ast) : \mathit{module} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  If there exists a derivation for the source `\mathit{char}^\ast` as a `\mathtt{module}` according to the text grammar for modules, yielding a module `m`, then return `m`.

2.  Else, return `\mathsf{error}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{module\_parse}(c^\ast) &=& m && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathtt{module} \stackrel\ast\Longrightarrow m{:}c^\ast) \\
    \mathrm{module\_parse}(c^\ast) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{module\_validate}(\mathit{module}) : \mathit{error}^?`

1.  If `\mathit{module}` is valid, then return nothing.

2.  Else, return `\mathsf{error}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{module\_validate}(m) &=& \epsilon && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} {} \vdash m : \mathit{externtype}^\ast \rightarrow {\mathit{externtype}'}^\ast) \\
    \mathrm{module\_validate}(m) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{module\_instantiate}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{module}, \mathit{externaddr}^\ast) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{moduleinst} ~|~ \mathit{exception} ~|~ \mathit{error})`

1.  Try instantiating `\mathit{module}` in `\mathit{store}` with external addresses `\mathit{externaddr}^\ast` as imports:

> 1.  If it succeeds with a module instance `\mathit{moduleinst}`, then let `\mathit{result}` be `\mathit{moduleinst}`.
>
> 2.  Else, let `\mathit{result}` be `\mathsf{error}`.

1.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{result}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{module\_instantiate}(S, m, \mathit{ev}^\ast) &=& (S', F.\mathsf{module}) && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{instantiate}(S, m, \mathit{ev}^\ast) \hookrightarrow^\ast S'; F; \epsilon) \\
    \mathrm{module\_instantiate}(S, m, \mathit{ev}^\ast) &=& (S', \mathsf{error}) && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}, \mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{instantiate}(S, m, \mathit{ev}^\ast) \hookrightarrow^\ast S'; F; \mathit{result}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

The store may be modified even in case of an error.

### `\mathrm{module\_imports}(\mathit{module}) : (\mathit{name}, \mathit{name}, \mathit{externtype})^\ast`

1.  Pre-condition: `\mathit{module}` is valid with the external import types `\mathit{externtype}^\ast` and external export types `{\mathit{externtype}'}^\ast`.

2.  Let `\mathit{import}^\ast` be the imports of `\mathit{module}`.

3.  Assert: the length of `\mathit{import}^\ast` equals the length of `\mathit{externtype}^\ast`.

4.  For each `\mathit{import}_i` in `\mathit{import}^\ast` and corresponding `\mathit{externtype}_i` in `\mathit{externtype}^\ast`, do:

> 1.  Let `\mathsf{import}~\mathit{nm}_{i1}~\mathit{nm}_{i2}~\mathit{xt}_i` be the deconstruction of `\mathit{import}_i`.
>
> 2.  Let `\mathit{result}_i` be the triple `(\mathit{nm}_{i1}, \mathit{nm}_{i2}, \mathit{externtype}_i)`.

1.  Return the concatenation of all `\mathit{result}_i`, in index order.

2.  Post-condition: each `\mathit{externtype}_i` is valid under the empty context.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{module\_imports}(m) &=& (\mathit{nm}_1, \mathit{nm}_2, \mathit{externtype})^\ast \\
    && \qquad (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} (\mathsf{import}~\mathit{nm}_1~\mathit{nm}_2~\mathit{xt}^\ast)^\ast \in m \wedge {} \vdash m : \mathit{externtype}^\ast \rightarrow {\mathit{externtype}'}^\ast) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{module\_exports}(\mathit{module}) : (\mathit{name}, \mathit{externtype})^\ast`

1.  Pre-condition: `\mathit{module}` is valid with the external import types `\mathit{externtype}^\ast` and external export types `{\mathit{externtype}'}^\ast`.

2.  Let `\mathit{export}^\ast` be the exports of `\mathit{module}`.

3.  Assert: the length of `\mathit{export}^\ast` equals the length of `{\mathit{externtype}'}^\ast`.

4.  For each `\mathit{export}_i` in `\mathit{export}^\ast` and corresponding `\mathit{externtype}'_i` in `{\mathit{externtype}'}^\ast`, do:

> 1.  Let `\mathsf{export}~\mathit{nm}_i~\mathit{externidx}_i` be the deconstruction of `\mathit{export}_i`.
>
> 2.  Let `\mathit{result}_i` be the pair `(\mathit{nm}_i, \mathit{externtype}'_i)`.

1.  Return the concatenation of all `\mathit{result}_i`, in index order.

2.  Post-condition: each `\mathit{externtype}'_i` is valid under the empty context.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{module\_exports}(m) &=& (\\mathit{nm}, \mathit{externtype}')^\ast \\
    && \qquad (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} (\mathsf{export}~\mathit{nm}~\mathit{xt}^\ast)^\ast \in m \wedge {} \vdash m : \mathit{externtype}^\ast \rightarrow {\mathit{externtype}'}^\ast) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Module Instances

### `\mathrm{instance\_export}(\mathit{moduleinst}, \mathit{name}) : \mathit{externaddr} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Assert: due to validity of the module instance `\mathit{moduleinst}`, all its export names are different.

2.  If there exists an `\mathit{exportinst}_i` in `\mathit{moduleinst}.\mathsf{exports}` such that name `\mathit{exportinst}_i.\mathsf{name}` equals `\mathit{name}`, then:

    1.  Return the external address `\mathit{exportinst}_i.\mathsf{addr}`.

3.  Else, return `\mathsf{error}`.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{instance\_export}(m, \mathit{name}) &=& m.\mathsf{exports}[i].\mathsf{addr} && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} m.\mathsf{exports}[i].\mathsf{name} = \mathit{name}) \\
    \mathrm{instance\_export}(m, \mathit{name}) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Functions

### `\mathrm{func\_alloc}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{deftype}, \mathit{hostfunc}) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{funcaddr})`

1.  Pre-condition: the defined type `\mathit{deftype}` is valid under the empty context and expands to a function type.

2.  Let `\mathit{funcaddr}` be the result of allocating a host function in `\mathit{store}` with defined type `\mathit{deftype}`, host function code `\mathit{hostfunc}` and an empty module instance.

3.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{funcaddr}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{func\_alloc}(S, \mathit{dt}, \mathit{code}) &=& (S', \mathit{a})
    && (\begin{array}{@{}l@{}}
    \mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{allocfunc}(S, \mathit{dt}, \mathit{code}, \{\}) = S', \mathit{a}) \\
    \end{array} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

This operation assumes that `\mathit{hostfunc}` satisfies the pre- and post-conditions required for a function instance with type `\mathit{deftype}`.

Regular (non-host) function instances can only be created indirectly through module instantiation.

### `\mathrm{func\_type}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{funcaddr}) : \mathit{deftype}`

1.  Let `\mathit{deftype}` be the definedn type `S.\mathsf{funcs}[a].\mathsf{type}`.

2.  Return `\mathit{deftype}`.

3.  Post-condition: the returned defined type is valid and expands to a function type.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{func\_type}(S, a) &=& S.\mathsf{funcs}[a].\mathsf{type} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{func\_invoke}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{funcaddr}, \mathit{val}^\ast) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{val}^\ast ~|~ \mathit{exception} ~|~ \mathit{error})`

1.  Try invoking the function `\mathit{funcaddr}` in `\mathit{store}` with values `\mathit{val}^\ast` as arguments:

> 1.  If it succeeds with values `{\mathit{val}'}^\ast` as results, then let `\mathit{result}` be `{\mathit{val}'}^\ast`.
>
> 2.  Else if the outcome is an exception with a thrown exception `\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~\mathit{exnaddr}` as the result, then let `\mathit{result}` be `\mathsf{exception}~\mathit{exnaddr}`
>
> 3.  Else it has trapped, hence let `\mathit{result}` be `\mathsf{error}`.

1.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{result}`.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{func\_invoke}(S, a, v^\ast) &=& (S', {v'}^\ast) && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{invoke}(S, a, v^\ast) \hookrightarrow^\ast S'; F; {v'}^\ast) \\
    \mathrm{func\_invoke}(S, a, v^\ast) &=& (S', \mathsf{exception}~a') && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{invoke}(S, a, v^\ast) \hookrightarrow^\ast S'; F; (\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a')~\mathsf{throw\_ref} \\
    \mathrm{func\_invoke}(S, a, v^\ast) &=& (S', \mathsf{error}) && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{invoke}(S, a, v^\ast) \hookrightarrow^\ast S'; F; \mathsf{trap}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

The store may be modified even in case of an error.

## Tables

### `\mathrm{table\_alloc}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tabletype}, \mathit{ref}) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{tableaddr})`

1.  Pre-condition: the `\mathit{tabletype}` is valid under the empty context.

2.  Let `\mathit{tableaddr}` be the result of allocating a table in `\mathit{store}` with table type `\mathit{tabletype}` and initialization value `\mathit{ref}`.

3.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{tableaddr}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{table\_alloc}(S, \mathit{tt}, r) &=& (S', \mathit{a}) && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{alloctable}(S, \mathit{tt}, r) = S', \mathit{a}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{table\_type}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tableaddr}) : \mathit{tabletype}`

1.  Return `S.\mathsf{tables}[a].\mathsf{type}`.

2.  Post-condition: the returned table type is valid under the empty context.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{table\_type}(S, a) &=& S.\mathsf{tables}[a].\mathsf{type} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{table\_read}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tableaddr}, i:\mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}) : \mathit{ref} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Let `\mathit{ti}` be the table instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{tables}[\mathit{tableaddr}]`.

2.  If `i` is larger than or equal to the length of `\mathit{ti}.\mathsf{refs}`, then return `\mathsf{error}`.

3.  Else, return the reference value `\mathit{ti}.\mathsf{refs}[i]`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{table\_read}(S, a, i) &=& r && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S.\mathsf{tables}[a].\mathsf{refs}[i] = r) \\
    \mathrm{table\_read}(S, a, i) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{table\_write}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tableaddr}, i:\mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}, \mathit{ref}) : \mathit{store} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Let `\mathit{ti}` be the table instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{tables}[\mathit{tableaddr}]`.

2.  If `i` is larger than or equal to the length of `\mathit{ti}.\mathsf{refs}`, then return `\mathsf{error}`.

3.  Replace `\mathit{ti}.\mathsf{refs}[i]` with the reference value `\mathit{ref}`.

4.  Return the updated store.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{table\_write}(S, a, i, r) &=& S' && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S' = S \mathrel{\mbox{with}} \mathsf{tables}[a].\mathsf{refs}[i] = r) \\
    \mathrm{table\_write}(S, a, i, r) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{table\_size}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tableaddr}) : \mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}`

1.  Return the length of `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{tables}[\mathit{tableaddr}].\mathsf{refs}`.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{table\_size}(S, a) &=& n &&
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} |S.\mathsf{tables}[a].\mathsf{refs}| = n) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{table\_grow}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tableaddr}, n:\mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}, \mathit{ref}) : \mathit{store} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Try growing the table instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{tables}[\mathit{tableaddr}]` by `n` elements with initialization value `\mathit{ref}`:

    1.  If it succeeds, return the updated store.

    2.  Else, return `\mathsf{error}`.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{table\_grow}(S, a, n, r) &=& S' &&
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S' = S \mathrel{\mbox{with}} \mathsf{tables}[a] = \mathrm{growtable}(S.\mathsf{tables}[a], n, r)) \\
    \mathrm{table\_grow}(S, a, n, r) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Memories

### `\mathrm{mem\_alloc}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{memtype}) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{memaddr})`

1.  Pre-condition: the `\mathit{memtype}` is valid under the empty context.

2.  Let `\mathit{memaddr}` be the result of allocating a memory in `\mathit{store}` with memory type `\mathit{memtype}`.

3.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{memaddr}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{mem\_alloc}(S, \mathit{mt}) &=& (S', \mathit{a}) && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{allocmem}(S, \mathit{mt}) = S', \mathit{a}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{mem\_type}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{memaddr}) : \mathit{memtype}`

1.  Return `S.\mathsf{mems}[a].\mathsf{type}`.

2.  Post-condition: the returned memory type is valid under the empty context.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{mem\_type}(S, a) &=& S.\mathsf{mems}[a].\mathsf{type} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{mem\_read}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{memaddr}, i:\mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}) : \mathit{byte} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Let `\mathit{mi}` be the memory instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{mems}[\mathit{memaddr}]`.

2.  If `i` is larger than or equal to the length of `\mathit{mi}.\mathsf{bytes}`, then return `\mathsf{error}`.

3.  Else, return the byte `\mathit{mi}.\mathsf{bytes}[i]`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{mem\_read}(S, a, i) &=& b && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S.\mathsf{mems}[a].\mathsf{bytes}[i] = b) \\
    \mathrm{mem\_read}(S, a, i) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{mem\_write}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{memaddr}, i:\mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}, \mathit{byte}) : \mathit{store} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Let `\mathit{mi}` be the memory instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{mems}[\mathit{memaddr}]`.

2.  If `i` is larger than or equal to the length of `\mathit{mi}.\mathsf{bytes}`, then return `\mathsf{error}`.

3.  Replace `\mathit{mi}.\mathsf{bytes}[i]` with `\mathit{byte}`.

4.  Return the updated store.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{mem\_write}(S, a, i, b) &=& S' && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S' = S \mathrel{\mbox{with}} \mathsf{mems}[a].\mathsf{bytes}[i] = b) \\
    \mathrm{mem\_write}(S, a, i, b) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{mem\_size}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{memaddr}) : \mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}`

1.  Return the length of `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{mems}[\mathit{memaddr}].\mathsf{bytes}` divided by the page size.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{mem\_size}(S, a) &=& n &&
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} |S.\mathsf{mems}[a].\mathsf{bytes}| = n \cdot 64\,\mathrm{Ki}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{mem\_grow}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{memaddr}, n:\mathit{u\scriptstyle\kern-0.1em64}) : \mathit{store} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Try growing the memory instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{mems}[\mathit{memaddr}]` by `n` pages:

    1.  If it succeeds, return the updated store.

    2.  Else, return `\mathsf{error}`.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{mem\_grow}(S, a, n) &=& S' &&
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S' = S \mathrel{\mbox{with}} \mathsf{mems}[a] = \mathrm{growmem}(S.\mathsf{mems}[a], n)) \\
    \mathrm{mem\_grow}(S, a, n) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Tags

### `\mathrm{tag\_alloc}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tagtype}) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{tagaddr})`

1.  Pre-condition: `tagtype` is valid.

2.  Let `\mathit{tagaddr}` be the result of allocating a tag in `\mathit{store}` with tag type `\mathit{tagtype}`.

3.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{tagaddr}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{tag\_alloc}(S, \mathit{tt}) &=& (S', \mathit{a}) && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{alloctag}(S, \mathit{tt}) = S', \mathit{a}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{tag\_type}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tagaddr}) : \mathit{tagtype}`

1.  Return `S.\mathsf{tags}[a].\mathsf{type}`.

2.  Post-condition: the returned tag type is valid.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{tag\_type}(S, a) &=& S.\mathsf{tags}[a].\mathsf{type} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Exceptions

### `\mathrm{exn\_alloc}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{tagaddr}, \mathit{val}^\ast) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{exnaddr})`

1.  Pre-condition: `\mathit{tagaddr}` is an allocated tag address.

2.  Let `\mathit{exnaddr}` be the result of allocating an exception instance in `\mathit{store}` with tag address `\mathit{tagaddr}` and initialization values `\mathit{val}^\ast`.

3.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{exnaddr}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lcll}
    \mathrm{exn\_alloc}(S, \mathit{tagaddr}, \mathit{val}^\ast) &=& (S \oplus \{\mathsf{exns}~\mathit{exninst}\}, |S.\mathsf{exns}|) &
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathit{exninst} = \{\mathsf{tag}~\mathit{tagaddr}, \mathsf{fields}~\mathit{val}^\ast\} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{exn\_tag}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{exnaddr}) : \mathit{tagaddr}`

1.  Let `\mathit{exninst}` be the exception instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{exns}[\mathit{exnaddr}]`.

2.  Return the tag address `\mathit{exninst}.\mathsf{tag}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lcll}
    \mathrm{exn\_tag}(S, a) &=& \mathit{exninst}.\mathsf{tag} &
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathit{exninst} = S.\mathsf{exns}[a]) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{exn\_read}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{exnaddr}) : \mathit{val}^\ast`

1.  Let `\mathit{exninst}` be the exception instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{exns}[\mathit{exnaddr}]`.

2.  Return the values `\mathit{exninst}.\mathsf{fields}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lcll}
    \mathrm{exn\_read}(S, a) &=& \mathit{exninst}.\mathsf{fields} &
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathit{exninst} = S.\mathsf{exns}[a]) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Globals

### `\mathrm{global\_alloc}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{globaltype}, \mathit{val}) : (\mathit{store}, \mathit{globaladdr})`

1.  Pre-condition: the `\mathit{globaltype}` is valid under the empty context.

2.  Let `\mathit{globaladdr}` be the result of allocating a global in `\mathit{store}` with global type `\mathit{globaltype}` and initialization value `\mathit{val}`.

3.  Return the new store paired with `\mathit{globaladdr}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{global\_alloc}(S, \mathit{gt}, v) &=& (S', \mathit{a}) && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{allocglobal}(S, \mathit{gt}, v) = S', \mathit{a}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{global\_type}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{globaladdr}) : \mathit{globaltype}`

1.  Return `S.\mathsf{globals}[a].\mathsf{type}`.

2.  Post-condition: the returned global type is valid under the empty context.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{global\_type}(S, a) &=& S.\mathsf{globals}[a].\mathsf{type} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{global\_read}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{globaladdr}) : \mathit{val}`

1.  Let `\mathit{gi}` be the global instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{globals}[\mathit{globaladdr}]`.

2.  Return the value `\mathit{gi}.\mathsf{value}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{global\_read}(S, a) &=& v && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S.\mathsf{globals}[a].\mathsf{value} = v) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{global\_write}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{globaladdr}, \mathit{val}) : \mathit{store} ~|~ \mathit{error}`

1.  Let `\mathit{gi}` be the global instance `\mathit{store}.\mathsf{globals}[\mathit{globaladdr}]`.

2.  Let `\mathit{mut}~t` be the structure of the global type `\mathit{gi}.\mathsf{type}`.

3.  If `\mathit{mut}` is empty, then return `\mathsf{error}`.

4.  Replace `\mathit{gi}.\mathsf{value}` with the value `\mathit{val}`.

5.  Return the updated store.

    \begin{split}~ \\
    \begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{global\_write}(S, a, v) &=& S' && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S.\mathsf{globals}[a].\mathsf{type} = \mathsf{mut}~t \wedge S' = S \mathrel{\mbox{with}} \mathsf{globals}[a].\mathsf{value} = v) \\
    \mathrm{global\_write}(S, a, v) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Values

### `\mathrm{ref\_type}(\mathit{store}, \mathit{ref}) : \mathit{reftype}`

1.  Pre-condition: the reference `\mathit{ref}` is valid under store `S`.

2.  Return the reference type `t` with which `\mathit{ref}` is valid.

3.  Post-condition: the returned reference type is valid under the empty context.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{ref\_type}(S, r) &=& t && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} S \vdash r : t) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

In future versions of WebAssembly, not all references may carry precise type information at run time. In such cases, this function may return a less precise supertype.

### `\mathrm{val\_default}(\mathit{valtype}) : \mathit{val}`

1.  If `\mathrm{default}_{valtype}` is not defined, then return `\mathsf{error}`.

1.  Else, return the value `\mathrm{default}_{valtype}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{val\_default}(t) &=& v && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{default}_t = v) \\
    \mathrm{val\_default}(t) &=& \mathsf{error} && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{default}_t = \epsilon) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Matching

### `\mathrm{match\_valtype}(\mathit{valtype}_1, \mathit{valtype}_2) : \mathit{bool}`

1.  Pre-condition: the value types `\mathit{valtype}_1` and `\mathit{valtype}_2` are valid under the empty context.

2.  If `\mathit{valtype}_1` matches `\mathit{valtype}_2`, then return `\mathit{true}`.

3.  Else, return `\mathit{false}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{match\_reftype}(t_1, t_2) &=& \mathit{true} && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} {} \vdash t_1 \leq t_2) \\
    \mathrm{match\_reftype}(t_1, t_2) &=& \mathit{false} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

### `\mathrm{match\_externtype}(\mathit{externtype}_1, \mathit{externtype}_2) : \mathit{bool}`

1.  Pre-condition: the extern types `\mathit{externtype}_1` and `\mathit{externtype}_2` are valid under the empty context.

2.  If `\mathit{externtype}_1` matches `\mathit{externtype}_2`, then return `\mathit{true}`.

3.  Else, return `\mathit{false}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{lclll}
    \mathrm{match\_externtype}(\mathit{et}_1, \mathit{et}_2) &=& \mathit{true} && (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} {} \vdash \mathit{et}_1 \leq \mathit{et}_2) \\
    \mathrm{match\_externtype}(\mathit{et}_1, \mathit{et}_2) &=& \mathit{false} && (\mathrel{\mbox{otherwise}}) \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

# Profiles

To enable the use of WebAssembly in as many environments as possible, *profiles* specify coherent language subsets that fit constraints imposed by common classes of host environments. A host platform can thereby decide to support the language only under a restricted profile, or even the intersection of multiple profiles.

## Conventions

A profile modification is specified by decorating selected rules in the main body of this specification with a *profile annotation* that defines them as conditional on the choice of profile.

For that purpose, every profile defines a *profile marker*, an alphanumeric short-hand like `\def\mathdef1451#1{{\small{\mathrm{#1}}}}\mathdef1451{ABC}`. A profile annotation of the form `\def\mathdef1452#1{{{}^{\small{[{!}#1]}}}}\mathdef1452{\mathrm{ABC}~\mathrm{XYZ}}` on a rule indicates that this rule is *excluded* for either of the profiles whose marker is `\def\mathdef1453#1{{\small{\mathrm{#1}}}}\mathdef1453{ABC}` or `\def\mathdef1454#1{{\small{\mathrm{#1}}}}\mathdef1454{XYZ}`.

There are two ways of subsetting the language in a profile:

- *Syntactic*, by *omitting* a feature, in which case certain constructs are removed from the syntax altogether.

- *Semantic*, by *restricting* a feature, in which case certain constructs are still present but some behaviours are ruled out.

### Syntax Annotations

To omit a construct from a profile syntactically, respective productions in the grammar of the abstract syntax are annotated with an associated profile marker. This is defined to have the following implications:

1.  Any production in the binary or textual syntax that produces abstract syntax with a marked construct is omitted by extension.

2.  Any validation or execution rule that handles a marked construct is omitted by extension.

The overall effect is that the respective construct is no longer part of the language under a respective profile.

Note

For example, a “busy” profile marked `\def\mathdef1455#1{{\small{\mathrm{#1}}}}\mathdef1455{BUSY}` could rule out the `\mathsf{nop}` instruction by marking the production for it in the abstract syntax as follows:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{llcl}
    \def\mathdef1420#1{{}}\mathdef1420{instruction} & \mathit{instr} &::=&
    \dots \\
    & \def\mathdef1456#1{{{}^{\small{[{!}#1]}}}}\mathdef1456{\mathrm{BUSY}} &|& \mathsf{nop} \\
    &                           &|& \mathsf{unreachable} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

A rule may be annotated by multiple markers, which could be the case if a construct is in the intersection of multiple features.

### Semantics Annotations

To restrict certain behaviours in a profile, individual validation or reduction rules or auxiliary definitions are annotated with an associated marker.

This has the consequence that the respective rule is no longer applicable under the given profile.

Note

For example, an “infinite” profile marked `\def\mathdef1457#1{{\small{\mathrm{#1}}}}\mathdef1457{INF}` could define that growing memory never fails:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{llcl@{\qquad}l}
    & S; F; (\mathsf{i\scriptstyle32}.\mathsf{const}~n)~\mathsf{memory{.}grow}~x &\hookrightarrow& S'; F; (\mathsf{i\scriptstyle32}.\mathsf{const}~\mathit{sz})
    \\&&&
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}r@{~}l@{}}
    (\mathrel{\mbox{if}} & F.\mathsf{module}.\mathsf{mems}[x] = a \\
    \wedge & \mathit{sz} = |S.\mathsf{mems}[a].\mathsf{datas}|/64\,\mathrm{Ki} \\
    \wedge & S' = S \mathrel{\mbox{with}} \mathsf{mems}[a] = \mathrm{growmem}(S.\mathsf{mems}[a], n)) \\[1ex]
    \end{array}
    \\[1ex]
    \def\mathdef1458#1{{{}^{\small{[{!}#1]}}}}\mathdef1458{\mathrm{INF}} & S; F; (\mathsf{i\scriptstyle32}.\mathsf{const}~n)~\mathsf{memory{.}grow}~x &\hookrightarrow& S; F; (\mathsf{i\scriptstyle32}.\mathsf{const}~\mathrm{signed}_{32}^{-1}(-1))
    \end{array}\end{split}

### Properties

All profiles are defined such that the following properties are preserved:

- All profiles represent syntactic and semantic subsets of the full profile, i.e., they do not *add* syntax or *alter* behaviour.

- All profiles are mutually compatible, i.e., no two profiles subset semantic behaviour in inconsistent or ambiguous ways, and any intersection of profiles preserves the properties described here.

- Profiles do not violate soundness, i.e., all configurations valid under that profile still have well-defined execution behaviour.

Note

Tools are generally expected to handle and produce code for the full profile by default. In particular, producers should not generate code that *depends* on specific profiles. Instead, all code should preserve correctness when executed under the full profile.

Moreover, profiles should be considered static and fixed for a given platform or ecosystem. Runtime conditioning on the “current” profile is not intended and should be avoided.

## Defined Profiles

Note

The number of defined profiles is expected to remain small in the future. Profiles are intended for broad and permanent use cases only. In particular, profiles are not intended for language versioning.

### Full Profile (`{\small{\mathrm{FUL}}}`)

The *full* profile contains the complete language and all possible behaviours. It imposes no restrictions, i.e., all rules and definitions are active. All other profiles define sub-languages of this profile.

### Deterministic Profile (`{\small{\mathrm{DET}}}`)

The *deterministic* profile excludes all rules marked `\def\mathdef1459#1{{{}^{\small{[{!}#1]}}}}\mathdef1459{\mathrm{DET}}`. It defines a sub-language that does not exhibit any incidental non-deterministic behaviour:

- All NaN values generated by floating-point instructions are canonical and positive.

- All relaxed vector instructions have a fixed behaviour that does not depend on the implementation.

Even under this profile, the `\mathsf{memory{.}grow}` and `\mathsf{table{.}grow}` instructions technically remain non-deterministic, in order to be able to indicate resource exhaustion.

Note

In future versions of WebAssembly, new non-deterministic behaviour may be added to the language, such that the deterministic profile will induce additional restrictions.

# Implementation Limitations

Implementations typically impose additional restrictions on a number of aspects of a WebAssembly module or execution. These may stem from:

- physical resource limits,

- constraints imposed by the embedder or its environment,

- limitations of selected implementation strategies.

This section lists allowed limitations. Where restrictions take the form of numeric limits, no minimum requirements are given, nor are the limits assumed to be concrete, fixed numbers. However, it is expected that all implementations have “reasonably” large limits to enable common applications.

Note

A conforming implementation is not allowed to leave out individual *features*. However, designated subsets of WebAssembly may be specified in the future.

## Syntactic Limits

### Structure

An implementation may impose restrictions on the following dimensions of a module:

- the number of types in a module

- the number of functions in a module, including imports

- the number of tables in a module, including imports

- the number of memories in a module, including imports

- the number of globals in a module, including imports

- the number of tags in a module, including imports

- the number of element segments in a module

- the number of data segments in a module

- the number of imports to a module

- the number of exports from a module

- the number of sub types in a recursive type

- the subtyping depth of a sub type

- the number of fields in a structure type

- the number of parameters in a function type

- the number of results in a function type

- the number of parameters in a block type

- the number of results in a block type

- the number of locals in a function

- the number of instructions in a function body

- the number of instructions in a structured control instruction

- the number of structured control instructions in a function

- the nesting depth of structured control instructions

- the number of label indices in a `\mathsf{br\_table}` instruction

- the number of instructions in a constant expression

- the length of the array in a `\mathsf{array{.}new\_fixed}` instruction

- the length of an element segment

- the length of a data segment

- the length of a name

- the range of characters in a name

If the limits of an implementation are exceeded for a given module, then the implementation may reject the validation, compilation, or instantiation of that module with an embedder-specific error.

Note

The last item allows embedders that operate in limited environments without support for [Unicode](https://www.unicode.org/versions/latest/) to limit the names of imports and exports to common subsets like [ASCII](https://webstore.ansi.org/RecordDetail.aspx?sku=INCITS+4-1986%5bR2012%5d).

### Binary Format

For a module given in binary format, additional limitations may be imposed on the following dimensions:

- the size of a module

- the size of any section

- the size of an individual function’s code

- the size of a structured control instruction

- the size of an individual constant expression’s instruction sequence

- the number of sections

### Text Format

For a module given in text format, additional limitations may be imposed on the following dimensions:

- the size of the source text

- the size of any syntactic element

- the size of an individual token

- the nesting depth of folded instructions

- the length of symbolic identifiers

- the range of literal characters allowed in the source text

## Validation

An implementation may defer validation of individual functions until they are first invoked.

If a function turns out to be invalid, then the invocation, and every consecutive call to the same function, results in a trap.

Note

This is to allow implementations to use interpretation or just-in-time compilation for functions. The function must still be fully validated before execution of its body begins.

## Execution

Restrictions on the following dimensions may be imposed during execution of a WebAssembly program:

- the number of allocated module instances

- the number of allocated function instances

- the number of allocated table instances

- the number of allocated memory instances

- the number of allocated global instances

- the number of allocated tag instances

- the number of allocated structure instances

- the number of allocated array instances

- the number of allocated exception instances

- the size of a table instance

- the size of a memory instance

- the size of an array instance

- the number of frames on the stack

- the number of labels on the stack

- the number of values on the stack

If the runtime limits of an implementation are exceeded during execution of a computation, then it may terminate that computation and report an embedder-specific error to the invoking code.

Some of the above limits may already be verified during instantiation, in which case an implementation may report exceedance in the same manner as for syntactic limits.

Note

Concrete limits are usually not fixed but may be dependent on specifics, interdependent, vary over time, or depend on other implementation- or embedder-specific situations or events.

# Type Soundness

The type system of WebAssembly is *sound*, implying both *type safety* and *memory safety* with respect to the WebAssembly semantics. For example:

- All types declared and derived during validation are respected at run time; e.g., every local or global variable will only contain type-correct values, every instruction will only be applied to operands of the expected type, and every function invocation always evaluates to a result of the right type (if it does not diverge, throw an exception, or trap).

- No memory location will be read or written except those explicitly defined by the program, i.e., as a local, a global, an element in a table, or a location within a linear memory.

- There is no undefined behavior, i.e., the execution rules cover all possible cases that can occur in a valid program, and the rules are mutually consistent.

Soundness also is instrumental in ensuring additional properties, most notably, *encapsulation* of function and module scopes: no locals can be accessed outside their own function and no module components can be accessed outside their own module unless they are explicitly exported or imported.

The typing rules defining WebAssembly validation only cover the *static* components of a WebAssembly program. In order to state and prove soundness precisely, the typing rules must be extended to the *dynamic* components of the abstract runtime, that is, the store, configurations, and administrative instructions. \[1\]

## Contexts

In order to check rolled up recursive types, the context is locally extended with an additional component that records the sub type corresponding to each recursive type index within the current group of recursive types:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}rrl@{}l@{}}
    & {\mathit{context}} & ::= & \{ \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}l@{}}
    \dots ,  \mathsf{recs}~{{\mathit{subtype}}^\ast} \} \\
    \end{array} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

## Types

Well-formedness for extended type forms is defined as follows.

The type use `(\mathsf{rec} {.} i)` is valid if:

> - The recursive type `C{.}\mathsf{recs}{}[i]` exists.

    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}\displaystyle
    \frac{
    C{.}\mathsf{recs}{}[i] = {\mathit{st}}
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec} {.} i : \mathsf{ok}
    }
    \qquad
    \end{array}

The heap type `\mathsf{bot}` is always valid.

    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}\displaystyle
    \frac{
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{bot} : \mathsf{ok}
    }
    \qquad
    \end{array}

The value type `\mathsf{bot}` is always valid.

    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}\displaystyle
    \frac{
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{bot} : \mathsf{ok}
    }
    \qquad
    \end{array}

The recursive type `(\mathsf{rec}~{{\mathit{subtype}}^\ast})` is valid for `i` if:

> - Either:
>
>   > - The sub type sequence `{{\mathit{subtype}}^\ast}` is empty.
>
> - Or:
>
>   > - The sub type sequence `{{\mathit{subtype}}^\ast}` is of the form `{\mathit{subtype}}_1~{{\mathit{subtype}'}^\ast}`.
>   >
>   > - The sub type `{\mathit{subtype}}_1` is valid for `i`.
>   >
>   > - The recursive type `(\mathsf{rec}~{{\mathit{subtype}'}^\ast})` is valid for `i + 1`.

    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}\displaystyle
    \frac{
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec}~\epsilon : {\mathsf{ok}}{(i)}
    }
    \qquad
    \frac{
    C \vdash {\mathit{subtype}}_1 : {\mathsf{ok}}{(i)}
    \qquad
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec}~{{\mathit{subtype}}^\ast} : {\mathsf{ok}}{(i + 1)}
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec}~({\mathit{subtype}}_1~{{\mathit{subtype}}^\ast}) : {\mathsf{ok}}{(i)}
    }
    \qquad
    \end{array}

The sub type `(\mathsf{sub}~{\mathsf{final}^?}~{{\mathit{typeuse}}^\ast}~{\mathit{comptype}})` is valid for `i` if:

> - The length of `{{\mathit{typeuse}}^\ast}` is less than or equal to `1`.
>
> - For all `{\mathit{typeuse}}` in `{{\mathit{typeuse}}^\ast}`:
>
>   > - The type use `{\mathit{typeuse}}` is valid.
>   >
>   > - `{\mathit{typeuse}} \prec i` is true.
>   >
>   > - The sub type `{{\mathrm{unroll}}}_{C}({\mathit{typeuse}})` is of the form `(\mathsf{sub}~{{\mathit{typeuse}'}^\ast}~{\mathit{comptype}'})`.
>
> - `{{\mathit{comptype}'}^\ast}` is the concatenation of all such `{\mathit{comptype}'}`.
>
> - The composite type `{\mathit{comptype}}` is valid.
>
> - For all `{\mathit{comptype}'}` in `{{\mathit{comptype}'}^\ast}`:
>
>   > - The composite type `{\mathit{comptype}}` matches the composite type `{\mathit{comptype}'}`.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{@{}c@{}}\displaystyle
    \frac{
    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}
    {|{{\mathit{typeuse}}^\ast}|} \leq 1
    \qquad
    (C \vdash {\mathit{typeuse}} : \mathsf{ok})^\ast
    \qquad
    ({\mathit{typeuse}} \prec i)^\ast
    \\
    ({{\mathrm{unroll}}}_{C}({\mathit{typeuse}}) = \mathsf{sub}~{{\mathit{typeuse}'}^\ast}~{\mathit{comptype}'})^\ast
    \\
    C \vdash {\mathit{comptype}} : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    (C \vdash {\mathit{comptype}} \leq {\mathit{comptype}'})^\ast
    \end{array}
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{sub}~{\mathsf{final}^?}~{{\mathit{typeuse}}^\ast}~{\mathit{comptype}} : {\mathsf{ok}}{(i)}
    }
    \qquad
    \end{array}\end{split}

where:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}[t]{@{}lcl@{}l@{}}
    {{\mathrm{unroll}}}_{C}({\mathit{deftype}}) & = & {\mathrm{unroll}}({\mathit{deftype}}) \\
    {{\mathrm{unroll}}}_{C}({\mathit{typeidx}}) & = & {\mathrm{unroll}}(C{.}\mathsf{types}{}[{\mathit{typeidx}}]) \\
    {{\mathrm{unroll}}}_{C}(\mathsf{rec} {.} i) & = & C{.}\mathsf{recs}{}[i] \\[0.8ex]
    \mathsf{rec} {.} j \prec i & = & j < i \\
    {\mathit{typeuse}} \prec i & = & \mathsf{true} & \quad \mbox{otherwise} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

The new rules for recursive types and sub types complement the ones previously given, which only allowed regular type indices as supertypes. They define validity of rolled-up recursive types, like they occur in defined types, in turn needed to define validity of contexts. None of these rules are needed in the implementation of a validator.

The defined type `({\mathit{rectype}} {.} i)` is valid if:

> - Let `{C'}` be the same context as `C`, but with the sub type sequence `{{\mathit{subtype}}^{n}}` prepended to the field `\mathsf{recs}`.
>
> - Under the context `{C'}`, the recursive type `{\mathit{rectype}}` is valid for `0`.
>
> - The recursive type `{\mathit{rectype}}` is of the form `(\mathsf{rec}~{{\mathit{subtype}}^{n}})`.
>
> - `i` is less than `n`.

    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}\displaystyle
    \frac{
    C, \mathsf{recs}~{{\mathit{subtype}}^{n}} \vdash {\mathit{rectype}} : {\mathsf{ok}}{(0)}
    \qquad
    {\mathit{rectype}} = \mathsf{rec}~{{\mathit{subtype}}^{n}}
    \qquad
    i < n
    }{
    C \vdash {\mathit{rectype}} {.} i : \mathsf{ok}
    }
    \qquad
    \end{array}

## Subtyping

Inside a rolled-up recursive type, a recursive type index can match another heap type.

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{@{}c@{}}\displaystyle
    \frac{
    C{.}\mathsf{recs}{}[i] = \mathsf{sub}~{\mathsf{final}^?}~(\mathsf{struct}~{{\mathit{fieldtype}}^\ast})
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec} {.} i \leq \mathsf{struct}
    }
    \\[3ex]\displaystyle
    \frac{
    C{.}\mathsf{recs}{}[i] = \mathsf{sub}~{\mathsf{final}^?}~(\mathsf{array}~{\mathit{fieldtype}})
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec} {.} i \leq \mathsf{array}
    }
    \\[3ex]\displaystyle
    \frac{
    C{.}\mathsf{recs}{}[i] = \mathsf{sub}~{\mathsf{final}^?}~(\mathsf{func}~{t_1^\ast} \rightarrow {t_2^\ast})
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec} {.} i \leq \mathsf{func}
    }
    \\[3ex]\displaystyle
    \frac{
    C{.}\mathsf{recs}{}[i] = \mathsf{sub}~{\mathsf{final}^?}~{{\mathit{typeuse}}^\ast}~{\mathit{ct}}
    }{
    C \vdash \mathsf{rec} {.} i \leq {{\mathit{typeuse}}^\ast}{}[j]
    }
    \qquad
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

These rules complement the previously given rules for matching heap types. They are only invoked when checking validity of rolled-up recursive types.

## Results

Results can be classified by result types as follows.

### Results `\mathit{val}^\ast`

- For each value `\mathit{val}_i` in `\mathit{val}^\ast`:

  - The value `\mathit{val}_i` is valid with some value type `t_i`.

- Let `t^\ast` be the concatenation of all `t_i`.

- Then the result is valid with result type `[t^\ast]`.

    \frac{
    (S \vdash \mathit{val} : t)^\ast
    }{
    S \vdash \mathit{val}^\ast : [t^\ast]
    }

### Results `(\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a)~\mathsf{throw\_ref}`

- The value `\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a` must be valid.

- Then the result is valid with result type `[t^\ast]`, for any valid closed result types.

    \frac{
    S \vdash \mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a : \mathsf{ref}~\mathsf{exn}
    \qquad
    \vdash [t^\ast] : \mathsf{ok}
    }{
    S \vdash (\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a)~\mathsf{throw\_ref} : [t^\ast]
    }

### Results `\mathsf{trap}`

- The result is valid with result type `[t^\ast]`, for any valid closed result types.

    \frac{
    \vdash [t^\ast] : \mathsf{ok}
    }{
    S \vdash \mathsf{trap} : [t^\ast]
    }

## Store Validity

The following typing rules specify when a runtime store `S` is *valid*. A valid store must consist of tag, global, memory, table, function, data, element, structure, array, exception, and module instances that are themselves valid, relative to `S`.

To that end, each kind of instance is classified by a respective tag, global, memory, table, function, or element, type, or just `\mathsf{ok}` in the case of data structures, arrays, or exceptions. Module instances are classified by *module contexts*, which are regular contexts repurposed as module types describing the index spaces defined by a module.

### Store `S`

- Each tag instance `\mathit{taginst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{tags}` must be valid with some tag type `\mathit{tagtype}_i`.

- Each global instance `\mathit{globalinst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{globals}` must be valid with some global type `\mathit{globaltype}_i`.

- Each memory instance `\mathit{meminst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{mems}` must be valid with some memory type `\mathit{memtype}_i`.

- Each table instance `\mathit{tableinst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{tables}` must be valid with some table type `\mathit{tabletype}_i`.

- Each function instance `\mathit{funcinst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{funcs}` must be valid with some defined type `\mathit{deftype}_i`.

- Each data instance `\mathit{datainst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{datas}` must be valid.

- Each element instance `\mathit{eleminst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{elems}` must be valid with some reference type `\mathit{reftype}_i`.

- Each structure instance `\mathit{structinst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{structs}` must be valid.

- Each array instance `\mathit{arrayinst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{arrays}` must be valid.

- Each exception instance `\mathit{exninst}_i` in `S.\mathsf{exns}` must be valid.

- No reference to a bound structure address must be reachable from itself through a path consisting only of indirections through immutable structure, or array fields or fields of exception instances.

- No reference to a bound array address must be reachable from itself through a path consisting only of indirections through immutable structure or array fields or fields of exception instances.

- No reference to a bound exception address must be reachable from itself through a path consisting only of indirections through immutable structure or array fields or fields of exception instances.

- Then the store is valid.

    \begin{split}~\\[-1ex]
    \frac{
    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}
    (S \vdash \mathit{taginst} : \mathit{tagtype})^\ast
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{globalinst} : \mathit{globaltype})^\ast
    \\
    (S \vdash \mathit{meminst} : \mathit{memtype})^\ast
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{tableinst} : \mathit{tabletype})^\ast
    \\
    (S \vdash \mathit{funcinst} : \mathit{deftype})^\ast
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{datainst} : \mathsf{ok})^\ast
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{eleminst} : \mathit{reftype})^\ast
    \\
    (S \vdash \mathit{structinst} : \mathsf{ok})^\ast
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{arrayinst} : \mathsf{ok})^\ast
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{exninst} : \mathsf{ok})^\ast
    \\
    S = \{
    \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
    \mathsf{tags}~\mathit{taginst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{globals}~\mathit{globalinst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{mems}~\mathit{meminst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{tables}~\mathit{tableinst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{funcs}~\mathit{funcinst}^\ast, \\
    \mathsf{datas}~\mathit{datainst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{elems}~\mathit{eleminst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{structs}~\mathit{structinst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{arrays}~\mathit{arrayinst}^\ast,
    \mathsf{exns}~\mathit{exninst}^\ast \}
    \end{array}
    \\
    (S.\mathsf{structs}[a_{\mathrm{s}}] = \mathit{structinst})^\ast
    \qquad
    ((\mathsf{ref{.}struct}~a_{\mathrm{s}}) \not\gg^+_S (\mathsf{ref{.}struct}~a_{\mathrm{s}}))^\ast
    \\
    (S.\mathsf{arrays}[a_{\mathrm{a}}] = \mathit{arrayinst})^\ast
    \qquad
    ((\mathsf{ref{.}array}~a_{\mathrm{a}}) \not\gg^+_S (\mathsf{ref{.}array}~a_{\mathrm{a}}))^\ast
    \\
    (S.\mathsf{exns}[a_{\mathrm{e}}] = \mathit{exninst})^\ast
    \qquad
    ((\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a_{\mathrm{e}}) \not\gg^+_S (\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a_{\mathrm{e}}))^\ast
    \end{array}
    }{
    \vdash S : \mathsf{ok}
    }\end{split}

where `\mathit{val}_1 \gg^+_S \mathit{val}_2` denotes the transitive closure of the following *immutable reachability* relation on values:

    \begin{split}\begin{array}{@{}lcll@{}}
    (\mathsf{ref{.}struct}~a) &\gg_S& S.\mathsf{structs}[a].\mathsf{fields}[i]
    & \mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{expand}(S.\mathsf{structs}[a].\mathsf{type}) = \mathsf{struct}~\mathit{ft}_1^i~\mathit{st}~\mathit{ft}_2^\ast \\
    (\mathsf{ref{.}array}~a) &\gg_S& S.\mathsf{arrays}[a].\mathsf{fields}[i]
    & \mathrel{\mbox{if}} \mathrm{expand}(S.\mathsf{arrays}[a].\mathsf{type}) = \mathsf{array}~\mathit{st} \\
    (\mathsf{ref{.}exn}~a) &\gg_S& S.\mathsf{exns}[a].\mathsf{fields}[i] \\
    (\mathsf{ref{.}extern}~\mathit{ref}) &\gg_S& \mathit{ref} \\
    \end{array}\end{split}

Note

The constraint on reachability through immutable fields prevents the presence of cyclic data structures that can not be constructed in the language. Cycles can only be formed using mutation.

### Tag Instances `\{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{tagtype} \}`

- The tag type `\mathit{tagtype}` must be valid under the empty context.

- Then the tag instance is valid with tag type `\mathit{tagtype}`.

    \frac{
    \vdash \mathit{tagtype} : \mathsf{ok}
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{tagtype} \} : \mathit{tagtype}
    }

### Global Instances `\{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{mut}~t, \mathsf{value}~\mathit{val} \}`

- The global type `\mathit{mut}~t` must be valid under the empty context.

- The value `\mathit{val}` must be valid with some value type `t'`.

- The value type `t'` must match the value type `t`.

- Then the global instance is valid with global type `\mathit{mut}~t`.

    \frac{
    \vdash \mathit{mut}~t : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    S \vdash \mathit{val} : t'
    \qquad
    \vdash t' \leq t
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{mut}~t, \mathsf{value}~\mathit{val} \} : \mathit{mut}~t
    }

### Memory Instances `\{ \mathsf{type}~(\mathit{addrtype}~\mathit{limits}), \mathsf{bytes}~b^\ast \}`

- The memory type `\mathit{addrtype}~\mathit{limits}` must be valid under the empty context.

- Let `\mathit{limits}` be `[n\,{..}\,m]`.

- The length of `b^\ast` must equal `m` multiplied by the page size `64\,\mathrm{Ki}`.

- Then the memory instance is valid with memory type `\mathit{addrtype}~\mathit{limits}`.

    \frac{
    \vdash \mathit{addrtype}~[n\,{..}\,m] : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    |b^\ast| = n \cdot 64\,\mathrm{Ki}
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{type}~(\mathit{addrtype}~[n\,{..}\,m]), \mathsf{bytes}~b^\ast \} : \mathit{addrtype}~[n\,{..}\,m]
    }

### Table Instances `\{ \mathsf{type}~(\mathit{addrtype}~\mathit{limits}~t), \mathsf{refs}~\mathit{ref}^\ast \}`

- The table type `\mathit{addrtype}~\mathit{limits}~t` must be valid under the empty context.

- Let `\mathit{limits}` be `[n\,{..}\,m]`.

- The length of `\mathit{ref}^\ast` must equal `n`.

- For each reference `\mathit{ref}_i` in the table’s elements `\mathit{ref}^n`:

  - The reference `\mathit{ref}_i` must be valid with some reference type `t'_i`.

  - The reference type `t'_i` must match the reference type `t`.

- Then the table instance is valid with table type `\mathit{addrtype}~\mathit{limits}~t`.

    \frac{
    \vdash \mathit{addrtype}~[n\,{..}\,m]~t : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    |\mathit{ref}^\ast| = n
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{ref} : t')^\ast
    \qquad
    (\vdash t' \leq t)^\ast
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{type}~(\mathit{addrtype}~[n\,{..}\,m]~t), \mathsf{refs}~\mathit{ref}^\ast \} : \mathit{addrtype}~[n\,{..}\,m]~t
    }

### Function Instances `\{\mathsf{type}~\mathit{deftype}, \mathsf{module}~\mathit{moduleinst}, \mathsf{code}~\mathit{func}\}`

- The defined type `\mathit{deftype}` must be valid under an empty context.

- The module instance `\mathit{moduleinst}` must be valid with some context `C`.

- Under context `C`:

  - The function `\mathit{func}` must be valid with some defined type `\mathit{deftype}'`.

  - The defined type `\mathit{deftype}'` must match `\mathit{deftype}`.

- Then the function instance is valid with defined type `\mathit{deftype}`.

    \begin{split}\frac{
    \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}
    \vdash \mathit{deftype} : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    S \vdash \mathit{moduleinst} : C
    \\
    C \vdash \mathit{func} : \mathit{deftype}'
    \qquad
    C \vdash \mathit{deftype}' \leq \mathit{deftype}
    \end{array}
    }{
    S \vdash \{\mathsf{type}~\mathit{deftype}, \mathsf{module}~\mathit{moduleinst}, \mathsf{code}~\mathit{func}\} : \mathit{deftype}
    }\end{split}

### Host Function Instances `\{\mathsf{type}~\mathit{deftype}, \mathsf{hostfunc}~\mathit{hf}\}`

- The defined type `\mathit{deftype}` must be valid under an empty context.

- The expansion of defined type `\mathit{deftype}` must be some function type `\mathsf{func}~[t_1^\ast] \rightarrow [t_2^\ast]`.

- For every valid store `S_1` extending `S` and every sequence `\mathit{val}^\ast` of values whose types coincide with `t_1^\ast`:

  - Executing `\mathit{hf}` in store `S_1` with arguments `\mathit{val}^\ast` has a non-empty set of possible outcomes.

  - For every element `R` of this set:

    - Either `R` must be `\bot` (i.e., divergence).

    - Or `R` consists of a valid store `S_2` extending `S_1` and a result `\mathit{result}` whose type coincides with `[t_2^\ast]`.

- Then the function instance is valid with defined type `\mathit{deftype}`.

    \begin{split}\frac{
    \begin{array}[b]{@{}r@{}}
    \vdash \mathit{deftype} : \mathsf{ok}
    \\
    \mathit{deftype} \approx \mathsf{func}~ [t_1^\ast] \rightarrow [t_2^\ast]
    \end{array}
    \quad
    \begin{array}[b]{@{}l@{}}
    \forall S_1, \mathit{val}^\ast,~
    {\vdash S_1 : \mathsf{ok}} \wedge
    {\vdash S \preceq S_1} \wedge
    {S_1 \vdash \mathit{val}^\ast : [t_1^\ast]}
    \Longrightarrow {} \\ \qquad
    \mathit{hf}(S_1; \mathit{val}^\ast) \supset \emptyset \wedge {} \\ \qquad
    \forall R \in \mathit{hf}(S_1; \mathit{val}^\ast),~
    R = \bot \vee {} \\ \qquad\qquad
    \exists S_2, \mathit{result},~
    {\vdash S_2 : \mathsf{ok}} \wedge
    {\vdash S_1 \preceq S_2} \wedge
    {S_2 \vdash \mathit{result} : [t_2^\ast]} \wedge
    R = (S_2; \mathit{result})
    \end{array}
    }{
    S \vdash \{\mathsf{type}~\mathit{deftype}, \mathsf{hostfunc}~\mathit{hf}\} : \mathit{deftype}
    }\end{split}

Note

This rule states that, if appropriate pre-conditions about store and arguments are satisfied, then executing the host function must satisfy appropriate post-conditions about store and results. The post-conditions match the ones in the execution rule for invoking host functions.

Any store under which the function is invoked is assumed to be an extension of the current store. That way, the function itself is able to make sufficient assumptions about future stores.

### Data Instances `\{ \mathsf{bytes}~b^\ast \}`

- The data instance is valid.

    \frac{
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{bytes}~b^\ast \} : \mathsf{ok}
    }

### Element Instances `\{ \mathsf{type}~t, \mathsf{refs}~\mathit{ref}^\ast \}`

- The reference type `t` must be valid under the empty context.

- For each reference `\mathit{ref}_i` in the elements `\mathit{ref}^n`:

  - The reference `\mathit{ref}_i` must be valid with some reference type `t'_i`.

  - The reference type `t'_i` must match the reference type `t`.

- Then the element instance is valid with reference type `t`.

    \frac{
    \vdash t : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{ref} : t')^\ast
    \qquad
    (\vdash t' \leq t)^\ast
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{type}~t, \mathsf{refs}~\mathit{ref}^\ast \} : t
    }

### Structure Instances `\{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{deftype}, \mathsf{fields}~\mathit{fieldval}^\ast \}`

- The defined type `\mathit{deftype}` must be valid under the empty context.

- The expansion of `\mathit{deftype}` must be a structure type `\mathsf{struct}~\mathit{fieldtype}^\ast`.

- The length of the sequence of field values `\mathit{fieldval}^\ast` must be the same as the length of the sequence of field types `\mathit{fieldtype}^\ast`.

- For each field value `\mathit{fieldval}_i` in `\mathit{fieldval}^\ast` and corresponding field type `\mathit{fieldtype}_i` in `\mathit{fieldtype}^\ast`:

  - Let `\mathit{fieldtype}_i` be `\mathit{mut}~\mathit{storagetype}_i`.

  - The field value `\mathit{fieldval}_i` must be valid with storage type `\mathit{storagetype}_i`.

- Then the structure instance is valid.

    \frac{
    \vdash \mathit{dt} : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    \mathrm{expand}(\mathit{dt}) = \mathsf{struct}~(\mathit{mut}~\mathit{st})^\ast
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{fv} : \mathit{st})^\ast
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{dt}, \mathsf{fields}~\mathit{fv}^\ast \} : \mathsf{ok}
    }

### Array Instances `\{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{deftype}, \mathsf{fields}~\mathit{fieldval}^\ast \}`

- The defined type `\mathit{deftype}` must be valid under the empty context.

- The expansion of `\mathit{deftype}` must be an array type `\mathsf{array}~\mathit{fieldtype}`.

- Let `\mathit{fieldtype}` be `\mathit{mut}~\mathit{storagetype}`.

- For each field value `\mathit{fieldval}_i` in `\mathit{fieldval}^\ast`:

  - The field value `\mathit{fieldval}_i` must be valid with storage type `\mathit{storagetype}`.

- Then the array instance is valid.

    \frac{
    \vdash \mathit{dt} : \mathsf{ok}
    \qquad
    \mathrm{expand}(\mathit{dt}) = \mathsf{array}~(\mathit{mut}~\mathit{st})
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{fv} : \mathit{st})^\ast
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{type}~\mathit{dt}, \mathsf{fields}~\mathit{fv}^\ast \} : \mathsf{ok}
    }

### Field Values `\mathit{fieldval}`

- If `\mathit{fieldval}` is a value `\mathit{val}`, then:

  - The value `\mathit{val}` must be valid with value type `t`.

  - Then the field value is valid with value type `t`.

- Else, `\mathit{fieldval}` is a packed value `\mathit{packval}`:

  - Let `\mathit{packtype}.\mathsf{pack}~i` be the field value `\mathit{fieldval}`.

  - Then the field value is valid with packed type `\mathit{packtype}`.

    \frac{
    }{
    S \vdash \mathit{pt}.\mathsf{pack}~i : \mathit{pt}
    }

### Exception Instances `\{ \mathsf{tag}~a, \mathsf{fields}~\mathit{val}^\ast \}`

- The store entry `S.\mathsf{tags}[a]` must exist.

- The expansion of the tag type `S.\mathsf{tags}[a].\mathsf{type}` must be some function type `\mathsf{func}~[t^\ast] \rightarrow [{t'}^\ast]`.

- The result type `[{t'}^\ast]` must be empty.

- The sequence `\mathit{val}^ast` of values must have the same length as the sequence `t^\ast` of value types.

- For each value `\mathit{val}_i` in `\mathit{val}^ast` and corresponding value type `t_i` in `t^\ast`, the value `\mathit{val}_i` must be valid with type `t_i`.

- Then the exception instance is valid.

    \frac{
    S.\mathsf{tags}[a].\mathsf{type} \approx \mathsf{func}~ [t^\ast] \rightarrow []
    \qquad
    (S \vdash \mathit{val} : t)^\ast
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{tag}~a, \mathsf{fields}~\mathit{val}^\ast \} : \mathsf{ok}
    }

### Export Instances `\{ \mathsf{name}~\mathit{name}, \mathsf{addr}~\mathit{externaddr} \}`

- The external address `\mathit{externaddr}` must be valid with some external type `\mathit{externtype}`.

- Then the export instance is valid.

    \frac{
    S \vdash \mathit{externaddr} : \mathit{externtype}
    }{
    S \vdash \{ \mathsf{name}~\mathit{name}, \mathsf{addr}~\mathit{externaddr} \} : \mathsf{ok}
    }

### Module Instances `\mathit{moduleinst}`

- Each defined type `\mathit{deftype}_i` in `\mathit{moduleinst}.\mathsf{types}` must be valid under the empty context.

- For each tag address `\mathit{tagaddr}_i` in `\mathit{moduleinst}.\mathsf{tags}`, the external address `\mathsf{tag}~\mathit{tagaddr}_i` must be valid with some external type `\mathsf{tag}~\mathit{tagtype}_i`.

- For each global address `\mathit{globaladdr}_i` in `\mathit{moduleinst}.\mathsf{globals}`, the external address `\mathsf{global}~\mathit{globaladdr}_i` must be valid with some external type `\mathsf{global}~\mathit{globaltype}_i`.

- For each memory address `\mathit{memaddr}_i` in `\mathit{moduleinst}.\mathsf{mems}`, the external address `\mathsf{mem}~\mathit{memaddr}_i` must be valid with some external type `\mathsf{mem}~\mathit{memtype}_i`.
